title: Rāga Bahār
summary: Bahār's ascent and descent with four svara-vistāras, and a note on how Pathak ji's pause signs differ from other books. Śloka 126 then sets the order of work: free ālāpa, ālāpa in rhythm (layālāpa), free tānas, and finally tānas set in tāla, like cotton spun into thread and woven into cloth.

blocks.text: Sa Ma G̲a̲ Ma Pa G̲a̲ G̲a̲ Ma N̲i̲ Dha Ni (Ṡa| Ṡa – N̲i̲ Pa Ma Pa G̲a̲ Ma Re Sa|
(1) Sa Ma, G̲a̲ G̲a̲ Ma, Ma Pa G̲a̲ Ma G̲a̲ Ma G̲a̲ Ma Re Sa|
(2) G̲a̲ Ga N̲i̲ Pa G̲a̲ Ma, Ṡa – N̲i̲Pa G̲a̲ Ma, N̲i̲N̲i̲ MaPa G̲a̲ Ma, G̲a̲ Ma Re – Sa|
(3) G̲a̲ Ma N̲i̲ Dha N̲i̲ – Ni Ṡa, N̲i̲ Dha N̲i̲ – DhaNi Ṡa, Ni Ṡa Ṙe N̲i̲ Dha – DhaNi Ṡa Ṡa N̲i̲ Pa MaPa G̲a̲ G̲a̲ – Ma Re Sa|
(4) Sa Ma – Ma Pa G̲a̲, Ma N̲i̲, – Ṇ̲i̲ Dha Ṇ̲i̲ Dha Ni – Ṡa, NiṠa Re Ġ̲a̲ Ġ̲a̲, Ṁa Ṙe Ṡa, Ṡa – N̲i̲ Pa MaPa G̲a̲ G̲a̲ Ma – G̲a̲ MaRe – Sa|

Here the book has not been lengthened by giving the svara vistāra (elaboration of notes) of more rāgas, but the scientific basis of the method of ālāpa (svara vistāra) has been made clear. From the elaborations above it has become clear to us that the sign of nyāsa (resting note) and vinyāsa (phrase-ending note) can be used in the nyāsa, and the sign (mark) of vinyāsa in the vinyāsa. In other books nyāsa and vinyāsa have one and the same sign, e.g. - ṆiReGa, Ni Ma′ Re Ga, Re Ga Re Ma′ Ga and so on. But for apanyāsa (intermediate resting note) a sign of broken shape (khaṇḍākāra) has been given, e.g. - Ni Re Ga Ma′ Pa – Pa Ma′ Ga, Ga Ma′ Dha Pa – Re Ga and so on. For sanyāsa (ending note of the first phrase) all treatises give the sign of the full stop. So if, by the method described earlier, we understand the separate importance of the notes of rāgas and do the svara vistāra ourselves, and keep testing whether it is right or wrong by looking at the svara vistāras given in other books, it is possible that our sādhanā (practice) will succeed.

blocks.verse:
स्वरालापाल्लयालापो मुक्तान स्ततो भवेत्।
गीतादिषु समायुज्य तान्स्तालेन समभ्यसेत्।१२६।
blocks.text: From svarālāpa comes layālāpa, and from that the mukta tāna; joining these into songs and the like, one should practise them with the tāla.

Just as a bale of cotton is spread out and opened up, then given the form of thread and then made into cloth, after which the cloth is cut, sewn and so on according to one's various needs, and only then becomes fit for use - raw cotton by itself is used in only a few places - in the same way the ārohāvaroha (ascent and descent) form of a rāga is elaborated by the method of nyāsa and the rest, and then laya (tempo) is brought into that svara vistāra (elaboration of notes); this is called layālāpa (ālāpa in rhythm) or joḍ-ālāpa. Then, from it, on the basis of layakārī (rhythmic play) and the elements of tāna (tāna tattva), thread in the form of tānas is made. After that we are able to use them within a fixed tāla (metric cycle), together with tihāīs and so on. This is the meaning of the śloka above. As an example, three things are being presented in one rāga.
